 Judgment

1 By this judgment I will dispose of appeal u/sec.374 Cr.PC. filed on behalf of convict Pradeep Aggarwal against the judgment dated 18.12.2015 and order on sentence dated  Pradeep Aggarwal Vs. State 21.12.2015 passed by Ms. Priya Mahindra, then Ld.
ACMM-II, Patiala House Court, New Delhi.
2

The brief facts of the case as per record and from trial court record are that accused is running an establishment namely M/s Bikaner Mithai Wala at Shop No. 25, Central Road, Near Gurudwara Bhogal, New Delhi-110014.
On 23.12.2009 at about 4.00 p.m. Food Inspector Smt. Usha Kiran visited the said place and purchased 1500 grams of "Boondi Laddoo" (ready for sale) from accused.
FI was accompanied with SDM/LHA Ms. Juhi Mukherjee.
The said Boondi Laddoo was purchased for the purposes of analysis under PFA Act.
The same sample was divided into three parts, packed as per Rules of PFA.
Panchanama was prepared.
One sample was sent for analysis to Public Analyst.

As per the report of Analyst, sample did not confirm to the standard because "The sample is R/O 102 vs The State (Da) on 20 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/156768615/
1 adulterated because Total Dye Content of synthetic colour used exceeds the prescribed maximum limit of 100 PPM (147.80 PPM)."
3 As the sample was failed, prosecution was launched by Food Inspector by filing complaint dated 14.05.2010 with the court.
Accused was summoned.
He has exercised his right u/sec.13(2) PFA Act and get the sample analyzed by CFL.
CFL reported "I am of the opinion that the above sample contravenes Rule 30 of the PFA Rules 1955 (277.85 PPM)."

Pradeep Aggarwal Vs. State 4 Charge was framed against accused u/sec.2(ia) (a) (j)
(m) read with sec.7 of PFA Act, 1954 punishable u/sec.16(1A) of PFA Act.

5 After trial, vide judgment dated 18.12.2015 accused was convicted for offence u/sec.16(1A) of PFA Act and vide order on sentence dated 21.12.2015 was directed to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of 4 years and fine of Rs.2,000/- and in default of payment of fine SI of 15 days.
6

In this appeal, the accused has assailed the judgment on the following grounds:-
(i) Non-compliance of Sec.10(7) of PFA Act and Rule i.e. independent witnesses were not joined.
(ii) There is variation in PA report and CFL report which shows that the sample was not representative.

(iii) Non-compliance of Rule 14 of PFA Rules i.e. the bottles, spoon, tray were not made clean and dried at the spot by the food inspector or any other official.
(iv) After coming into Food Safety & Standards Act, the punishment is to be granted under the said Act (argued orally).
7
No reply was filed by respondent/state and the matter was argued orally.

8 I have gone through the record, Trial Court record and have heard the submissions of Ld. counsel for appellant and Ld. Pradeep Aggarwal Vs. State SPP for State.
9

sentences.text: It is argued by counsel for appellant that no public witness was present in the proceedings nor efforts were made to join any public witnesses.
As far as this argument is concerned, the same argument was raised before the Ld. Trial Court.
The same was dealt by the trial court from para 17 to 23 of the judgment.

As far as opinion/finding of the trial court regarding this argument is concerned, I do not find any infirmity in those findings and the same are upheld and the arguments regarding this fact does not find any force and thus rejected.

10 It is further argued that the sample was not representative and due to that reasons there is huge difference in the result in the reports of PA and CFL while conducting the same test on the same R/O 102 vs The State (Da) on 20 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/156768615/
2 sample commodity.
It is submitted by Ld. SPP for State that the samples were representative.
This leg of arguments was also done by the counsel for accused in the trial court and was dealt by the trial court from para 44 to 79 of the judgment.
I do not find any different opinion from that already given by the trial court hence the reasoning given by the trial court is upheld.
11 It is further argued that compliance u/sec.14 PFA Rules was not proved on record by the prosecution.

It is stated that witnesses are deposing differently with respect to the cleanliness of t r a y , s p o o n , b o t t l e s e t c . I t i s f u r t h e r s t a t e d t h a t i t w a s t h e d u t y o f
Pradeep Aggarwal Vs. State the prosecution to prove these facts
. These arguments were also addressed before the trial court.
The relevant part of the judgment dealing with these arguments are from para 24 to 35 of the judgment.
I have gone through the record and submissions forwarded.
As far as these witnesses are concerned, they have specifically stated that as to how the Ladoos were taken.
Even the Ladoos were taken from clean and dry tray, then weighed and even broken with the help of clean and dry steel spoon and that in clean and dry steel tray.

Thereafter,
they were put in clean and dry bottles.
There is no discrepancy in the testimony of the witnesses regarding these facts.
So, I do not find force in the arguments of Ld. counsel for appellant that there is non- compliance of Rule 14 PFA Rules, 1955.
So, in these circumstances, I do not find any ground for change/modification of Trial Court's judgment, on merits.
So, the finding of the trial court with respect to the conviction of accused u/sec.2(ia) (a) (j) & (m) of PFA Act 1954 read with Sec.16 of PFA Act, is upheld.
12 It is submitted by Ld. counsel for appellant that on the date of judgment/order on sentence, the PFA Act, 1954 was repealed.
It is further stated that the court should have passed the order on sentence as per the quantum/punishment mentioned in Food and Safety Standards Act, 2006 (hereinafter called FSSA).

For this purpose, Ld. counsel for appellant had relied on Judgment  Pradeep Aggarwal Vs. State i.e. Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan (Crl. Appeals No. 214 and 215 of 2016, vide order dated 10.03.2016, as corrected vide order dated 17.03.2016, as reported in 2016 (1) FAC 203) of Hon. Supreme Court and earlier judgment T Barai Vs. Henry, 1983 (1) SCC 177.
13

entities.text: Pradeep Aggarwal Vs. State i.e. Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan (Crl. Appeals No. 214 and 215 of 2016
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: On the other hand, it is argued by Ld. SPP for State that the sentencing cannot be done in new Act since the definition of many offences are changed in the new Act including this particular offence of which accused is charged.
Definition of major offences like "adulteration" and "misbranding" have been changed.

Now FSSA have definition "substandard food", "food containing extraneous matter",
"unsafe food" and "misbranded food".
Due to this reason, the ingredients have changed and thus there is no way in which the old offences could be related to new offences.

14 As far as the objection of Ld. SPP for State is concerned, in the present case, the offence was that the article/food i.e. Boondi Ladoo was found as being coloured with synthetic colour "Tartrazine and Sunset Yellow FCF" in excessive quantity than permitted by Rules.
This was violation of Rule 30 of PFA Rules and thus termed as adulteration in view of Sec.2(ia)(j) of PFA Act and thus consequently punishable u/sec.16(1) of PFA Act.
The charge was framed with these facts.

There was no  Pradeep Aggarwal Vs. State charge in which it is stated that the said colour was R/O 102 vs The State (Da) on 20 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/156768615/
3 injurious to health.
Had it been the case, the charge should have been u/sec.16(1-A) (ii) of PFA Act.
15 Now in the FSSA, such adulteration is termed as "sub- standard food" in terms of Sec.3(zx) of FSSA Act punishable u/sec.51 of FSSA.
So, if we go through both these provisions of law, a particular offence with a particular fact is mentioned with some other name but with same ingredients in the new FSSA Act.
16 Hence, it is held that it is the ingredients which constitute an offence, determines that whether it is the same offence but with new name or an altogether different offence.
Here the offence of adding excessive permissible synthetic colour than permitted in the food article which was punishable u/sec.16(ia) PFA Act is similar to the offence u/sec.51 of FSSA Act.
17 As far as the application of Nemi Chand judgment (supra) is concerned, the same is based on the old judgment i.e. T. Barai (supra) of Hon. Supreme Court.

The relevant portion of the T. Barai judgment is as follows:-
(Para 25) - It is settled both on authority and principle that when a later statute again describes an offence created by an earlier statute and imposes a different punishment, or varies the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by implication.
In M i c h e l l v . B r o w n [ ( 1 9 5 8 ) 1 2 0 E R 9 0 9 , 9 1 2 : 3 2 L T O S 1 4 6 : 7

sentences.text: Pradeep Aggarwal Vs. State WR 80] Lord Campbell put the matter thus:

"It is well settled rule of construction that, if a later statute again describes an offence created by a former statute and affixes a different punishment, varying the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by the later statute; see also Smith v. Benabo [(1937) 1 All ER 523: (1937) 1 KB 518: 156 LT 194] .

entities.text: Smith v. Benabo [(1937) 1 All ER 523: (1937) 1 KB 518: 156 LT 194]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In Regina v. Youle [(1861) 158 ER 311, 315-16: 4 LT 299: 9 WR 637] , Martin, B. said in the oft-quoted passage:
"If a statute deals with a particular class of offences, and a subsequent Act is passed which deals with precisely the same offences, and a different punishment is imposed by the later Act, I think that, in effect, the legislature has declared that the new Act shall be substituted for the earlier Act."
The rule is however subject to the limitation contained in Article 20(1) against ex post facto law providing for a greater punishment and has also no application where the offence described in the later Act is not the same as in the earlier Act i.e. when the essential ingredients of the two offences are different.

Moreover this particular aspect is stated as a illustration in the same judgment in para 23 which is as follows:-
R/O 102 vs The State (Da) on 20 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/156768615/
4

To illustrate, if Parliament were to reenact Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 and provide that the punishment for an offence of murder shall be sentence for imprisonment for life instead of the present sentence of death or imprisonment for life, then it cannot be that the courts would still award a sentence of death even in pending cases.
So, in these circumstances, it can be safely said that while considering on the point of sentence, the quantum of Pradeep Aggarwal Vs. State sentence in new Act i.e. FSSA is to be considered.

18 Now according to my aforesaid reasoning the offence of adding excessive permissible synthetic colour than permissible limit in food articles i.e. Boondi Ladoo, earlier punishable u/sec.16(i)(a) of PFA Act is to be considered as an offence u/sec.51 of FSSA Act for the purposes of awarding punishment.
The maximum punishment u/sec.51 FSSA Act is that of fine which may extend to Rs.5 lacs.
19 It is submitted by Ld. counsel for appellant that appellant is suffering the long pendency of trial and is a respectable person of society and have family.
So, lenient view be taken.
20 Opposed by Ld. SPP for State on the ground that the long duration of trial cannot be a ground for leniency.
21 I have gone through the rival contentions on this aspect.
22 After going through the entire arguments in this regard, accused/appellant Pradeep Aggarwal is directed to pay fine of Rs.2 lacs with the Trial Court.
In default of payment of fine, he is directed to undergo SI of 30 days.
23 Fine be deposited within 5 working days.

Fine already deposited with the trial court be adjusted.
